title: You're not perceiving the world, you're predicting it: your brain fabricates the reality you see
dek: Perception is not the passive receipt of external signals but a prediction the brain makes based on the body's internal state; the world and self you experience are a controlled hallucination constrained by sensory input, and all of it ultimately serves the maintenance of life.
why: A TED-style talk that uses three experiments — the checkerboard, noise, and the rubber hand — to explain predictive processing, and gives a clear answer to whether AI can be sentient. Good for beginners; light on cutting-edge detail.
who: Engineers working on AI consciousness or brain-computer interfaces, founders trying to judge whether AI will have self-awareness, and tech investors who need to distinguish intelligence from feeling.
skip: Listeners already familiar with predictive processing can skip the checkerboard and noise demos at 5:10-10:20 and go straight to the self section.

points.h: General anesthesia isn't sleep, it's complete nonexistence
points.body: The speaker disappeared completely for the third time during a general anesthetic: as the drug flooded his brain he felt detached, fragmented and cold, and then he woke up — but in between there was no sense of elapsed time at all. Waking from deep sleep you know how long you were out; waking from general anesthesia it could have been 5 minutes, 5 hours, 5 years or 50 years — he simply wasn't there. This complete disappearance is worth taking seriously because it turns "how does consciousness happen" into one of the biggest remaining puzzles in science and philosophy: how do billions of neurons produce the you of right now.

points.h: You see what your brain expects to see
points.body: The brain is locked inside the skull, with no light and no sound; all it gets is streams of electrical impulses that stand in only an indirect relationship to external objects. So perception is not a readout of the world but an informed guess: the brain combines sensory signals with prior expectations about what the world is "probably like" and guesses the most likely cause. In the checkerboard shadow illusion, squares A and B are exactly the same gray, but because the visual cortex knows a priori that "shadows darken surfaces," B is seen as brighter; the same meaningless noise suddenly resolves into words once you've heard the original sentence. The sensory input hasn't changed — only the brain's guess about its cause.

points.h: The world is generated from the inside out
points.body: Since perception is active guessing, the brain forms experience not only from sensory signals coming in from outside but equally, or even more, from predictions traveling inward. A Sussex team's demo processed campus footage with a Deep Dream-like algorithm to simulate what the brain sees when "prediction is too strong": dogs everywhere, the image turning into something like a hallucinatory state or the visual experience of psychosis. The conclusion is steep: if hallucination is perception out of control, then ordinary perception right now is also a hallucination — just a controlled one, in which the brain's predictions are held in check by sensory signals from the world.

points.h: The self is also a hallucination the brain generates
points.body: The experience of being "you" is likewise generated by the brain, and it isn't just one thing: there's the experience of having a body and of being a body, the experience of perceiving the world from a first-person perspective, the experience of intending to act and being the cause of events in the world, and the "distinct personality persisting over time" maintained by memory and social interaction. Psychiatry and neurology already know these dimensions can be pulled apart from one another. The supposedly unified, continuous self is actually a rather fragile construction of the brain, and like vision it requires explanation.

points.h: The brain will claim a fake hand as its own
points.body: The rubber hand illusion can be done at home: the real hand is hidden, a fake hand is placed in front of you, two brushes stroke the real and fake hands simultaneously, and the subject stares at the fake hand. After a while the fake hand vaguely becomes part of one's own body. The reason is that vision and touch agree, the shape looks like a hand, and the position is roughly where a hand should be — enough evidence for the brain to guess "this is my hand." Threaten the fake hand with a hammer and you can see the subject has taken it into their body. Sussex's Peter Lush found that the strength of the illusion correlates highly with hypnotic suggestibility: the experimental setup itself suggests "the fake hand belongs to you," so people who are easily suggestible naturally have that experience more readily.

points.h: A heartbeat in sync makes the fake hand feel more like your own
points.body: Besides viewing the body as an external object, the brain also senses the body from the inside, known as interoception: heartbeat, blood pressure and visceral states are constantly telling the brain what's going on internally. This kind of perception is often ignored, but it is precisely what keeps the body alive. In a VR version of the rubber hand experiment at the Sussex lab, the virtual hand flashed red and black either in sync or out of sync with the heartbeat; when in sync, subjects were markedly more likely to feel it was part of their own body. Body ownership is thus shown to be deeply rooted in the perception of the internal body.

points.h: Interoception isn't knowing, it's staying alive
points.body: Experience coming from inside the body is completely different from seeing the external world: you don't perceive "the kidney is here, the liver there, the spleen somewhere"; the viscera barely enter consciousness unless something goes wrong. That's because the brain's purpose in interoception is not to judge what is there but to control and regulate, holding physiological variables like blood pressure and heart rate within a narrow range suitable for survival. When prediction is used to identify external objects, we experience it as "seeing something"; when prediction is used to regulate the body, we experience it as whether control is going smoothly. So the most basic experience of self is rooted directly in the mechanisms that keep the organism alive.

points.h: A smarter computer is not a conscious one
points.body: Three consequences follow. First, since we can misperceive the world, we can also misperceive ourselves when prediction goes wrong; this gives psychiatry and neurology a chance to target mechanisms rather than only treating the symptoms of depression and schizophrenia. Second, "I am me" cannot be reduced to or uploaded into a software program running on some robot, no matter how smart or complex — we are creatures of flesh and blood, and conscious experience is shaped at every level by the biological mechanisms that maintain life. Third, everyone has their own inner universe, and human consciousness is just a small region in a vast space of possible consciousness. So merely making computers smarter will not make them sentient.

terms.def: The brain actively generates experience while being constrained by sensory signals; ordinary perception is a controlled hallucination.
The brain's perception of visceral states such as heartbeat and blood pressure, whose goal is not identification but regulation and survival.
Perception as the brain's guess about the causes of the world, combining sensory signals with prior expectations.

quotes.text: Consciousness and intelligence are very different things. You don't have to be smart to suffer, but you probably do have to be alive.
We don't just passively perceive our worlds. We actively generate them.
In fact, we're all hallucinating all the time, including right now. It's just that when we agree about our hallucinations, that's what we call reality.
Perception of the internal state of the body isn't about figuring out what's there. It's about control and regulation.
Just making computers smarter is not going to make them sentient.
